paragraphs: The earliest sound recordings of classical performers, made in the first decades of the twentieth century, preserve a style of playing that many modern listeners find disconcerting. Pianists of the period routinely sounded the notes of a chord one after another rather than together, and string players slid audibly from note to note in a manner that present-day conservatories discourage as sentimental. Because many of these performers had trained with musicians active in the mid-nineteenth century, the recordings would seem to offer precious evidence about how the music of that era was meant to sound.

Scholars have nonetheless hesitated to treat them as such. The recording process of the time, some argue, distorted performance: a single side of a disc could hold only about four minutes of sound, and performers playing into a horn that captured only loud, sharply defined sounds may have exaggerated certain effects. Yet the first of these constraints cuts in an unexpected direction. Pressure to fit a movement onto a single side would have encouraged faster tempos and fewer expressive liberties, not more. If anything, then, the recordings may understate the freedom with which these musicians ordinarily played.

After a city began requiring everyone who rents an electric scooter to wear a helmet, the number of scooter-related head injuries treated at the city's hospitals fell sharply. Over the same period, however, the total number of scooter-related injuries of all kinds treated at those hospitals fell by nearly the same proportion.

Museums have long judged their success by attendance, counting visitors at the door and paying little attention to what happens once they are inside. Studies that follow visitors through the galleries suggest that this measure misses a great deal. Visitors who use audio guides, for example, spend nearly twice as long in front of each work at which they stop, though they stop at fewer works overall. Because effects of this kind never appear in attendance figures, museums that report only those figures to their funders have had little reason to invest in such aids.

Among the most frequently cited generalizations in biogeography is the so-called island rule: when mammals colonize islands, large-bodied species tend to evolve smaller bodies and small-bodied species larger ones. The pattern has been explained in terms of the distinctive ecology of islands. Limited resources are thought to favor dwarfism in large herbivores, which can no longer sustain big bodies on small ranges, while the scarcity of predators and competitors is thought to release small mammals from the pressures that kept them small—the need to hide in narrow burrows, for instance, or to reproduce quickly before being eaten.

In recent decades, however, the rule's status has been contested. Several large comparative analyses have found that once the shared ancestry of related species is taken into account, the tendency toward intermediate body size on islands is weak or absent in many groups, and that the striking cases on which the rule was founded—dwarf elephants on Mediterranean islands, giant rats in the western Pacific—may be memorable precisely because they are exceptional. Critics also note that the rule's two halves are explained by different mechanisms, so that its apparent unity may be an artifact of grouping distinct phenomena under a single description.

Defenders of the rule reply that its critics have tested it too crudely. Island size, isolation, climate, and the time elapsed since colonization all vary enormously, and a pattern that holds strongly on small, remote islands with few predators may be diluted to statistical insignificance when such islands are pooled with large ones lying close to a mainland. On this view, the island rule is not false but conditional: a description of what tends to happen under circumstances that the global analyses fail to distinguish. Whether a generalization so qualified retains the explanatory power that made the original rule attractive is, of course, another question.

When a restaurant adds an extravagantly priced dish to its menu, sales of that dish are typically negligible. Yet restaurant consultants often recommend the practice, reporting that sales of the next most expensive items tend to rise afterward. The usual explanation is that diners judge prices relative to the other prices in view: beside a sixty-dollar entrée, a thirty-dollar one no longer seems extravagant. Skeptics point out that restaurants that add such dishes frequently revise the rest of their menus at the same time, so that the reported rise in sales cannot confidently be attributed to the expensive dish alone.

A survey of members of a national hiking club found that members who hike more than fifty miles a month report taking significantly fewer sick days from work than members who hike less. The club's newsletter concluded that frequent hiking strengthens the immune system and urged members to hike more often in order to stay healthy.
